nature-found-093.title: Why Nature does not maximise productivity
nature-found-093.text:
A portfolio manager would chase the highest yield. Nature does not. It maximises neither NPP, the net yearly growth of plant matter that feeds ecosystems, nor the regeneration rate of its ecosystems.

NPP per square metre differs by type of ecosystem: 0.75 kg a year in temperate grassy plains, 2.5 in {{ref:nature-eco-563}} and 0.14 in the ocean, because the abiotic environment varies. Even after allowing for that, planetary NPP is not at its maximum, and NPP in old growth forests is nearly zero. Life-form distributions emerged under selection pressures at the genetic level, not as an efficient spread of NPP. In the Review's fishery example, yield is zero at the long-run population K, so the {{ref:nature-econ-310}} of the {{ref:nature-res-049}} there is negative.

nature-found-097.title: Impact inequality: unequal incomes, unequal footprints
nature-found-097.text:
Two households with the same income can press on the biosphere very differently. {{ref:nature-hist-028}} therefore separates inequality in household incomes from inequality in impact, which is income corrected for the efficiency of converting nature into income.

Households differ in both income and that efficiency. A household's income divided by its efficiency (y/alpha) can be read as its {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, the demand idea from {{ref:nature-found-096}}. Across 136 countries the Review estimates footprint I = 0.97 y^0.41, where y is income per capita. One consequence follows: the global {{ref:nature-acct-027}} would be higher than today's if everyone received an equal share of today's global income.

nature-found-094.title: Regulating services work unseen until they fail
nature-found-094.text:
Mangroves yield visible timber and fish. Their protection of villages against storms is appreciated only after they are degraded, and it is far harder to value. That is the problem with regulating and maintenance services, the kind described in {{ref:nature-found-007}}: they are mostly hidden and silent, felt only over the long run or when they are lost.

Provisioning and cultural services are different, since their outcomes are readily detected even in the short run. A study of the 1999 Orissa super-cyclone found that villages protected by more mangroves suffered less property damage. The {{ref:nature-found-084}} of shrimp, then, should include the carbon sequestered by the mangroves cleared for shrimp farms and the protection they gave nearby communities.

nature-found-095.title: Why Nature's mobility and silence breed externalities
nature-found-095.text:
No one can contain the air they foul or the rivers they pollute. Externalities arise from the biosphere because {{ref:nature-econ-621}} to large parts of it are weakly defined or enforced, and because Nature is mobile, silent and invisible.

An {{ref:nature-found-031}} is an unaccounted-for consequence of one person's actions for others, including future people. The harm from fouled air or water is non-excludable. Nitrogen and phosphorus in an estuary aggregate leakages from innumerable distant fields, factories and households, so polluters do not pay for using it as a sink. No {{ref:nature-econ-621}} cover the oceans beyond national jurisdiction, so no one has an incentive to protect them from contamination or overfishing.

{{ref:nature-econ-633}} are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, a mirror image of {{ref:nature-econ-615}}. They are underproduced for the same reason that {{ref:nature-econ-615}} are overused.

nature-found-092.title: An asset's own rate of return
nature-found-092.text:
How much is one more unit of an asset worth tomorrow? The answer is its yield, or own rate of return: the growth expected tomorrow if one more unit is added to a portfolio today.

For produced capital, yield is its {{ref:nature-econ-310}}. For a fishery or a tree, it is the growth in biomass obtained by waiting. Investment can therefore be passive: restoring a wetland is investment, and so is conservation, which can simply mean waiting. Applied to {{ref:nature-found-010}}, the idea lets nature be compared with other assets.

Yield is a pure number per unit of time. The UK government's long-term bonds have historically averaged about 4% a year, though more recently closer to 1%. Because relative prices change unless the economy is stationary, own rates are not enough: the rate of return on an asset is its yield plus its capital gains over a unit of time.

nature-found-040.title: Environmental valuation: pricing what has no price
nature-found-040.text:
When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in. Environmental valuation tries to fix that by putting an {{ref:nature-econ-156}} on the environment and {{ref:nature-res-248}}, many of which have no market price. It draws on {{ref:nature-found-030}}, and it is one way to put numbers on {{ref:nature-found-010}} and on the harms described in {{ref:nature-found-031}}.

{{ref:nature-val-058}} can be read from behaviour, such as the cost of recreational trips or house prices in hedonic methods. {{ref:nature-val-069}} include {{ref:nature-val-054}}, {{ref:nature-val-055}} and {{ref:nature-val-053}}, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children. These are usually estimated with surveys such as {{ref:nature-val-085}} or {{ref:nature-val-091}}. {{ref:nature-val-085}} asks people what they would pay for an {{ref:nature-econ-647}}, or accept for its loss.

The stakes are practical. Without dollar values for benefits such as clean air and water, estimates of pollution-control benefits fall below true social benefits and policy chronically underinvests.

Valuation is controversial. Some environmentalists object to pricing what may be priceless, though such values keep society from ignoring nature in policy choices. {{ref:nature-econ-344}} is budget constrained and tends to be lower where incomes are lower, raising equity problems. {{ref:nature-val-089}} is not constrained and can in theory approach infinity.

nature-found-103.title: Biodiversity risk assessment: species and ecosystems at risk
nature-found-103.text: This is {{ref:nature-found-101}} applied to living diversity, with species {{ref:nature-eco-105}} or {{ref:nature-eco-632}} as the outcomes of concern. The units assessed are biological, such as species and populations, or ecological, such as habitats and ecosystems. Risks often relate to human threats and pressures. The {{ref:nature-acct-078}} was developed for biodiversity risk assessment, with collapse as the most extreme outcome.

nature-found-098.title: Persistent organic pollutants: chemicals that will not break down
nature-found-098.text:
Some chemicals released decades ago are still circulating in bodies and {{ref:nature-eco-297}}. Persistent organic pollutants, or POPs, are organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and photolytic degradation and are toxic to health and the environment. They are a hard case of the {{ref:nature-found-075}} and of {{ref:nature-found-055}}.

Most POPs are man-made {{ref:nature-hist-084}} or insecticides, plus some solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals. A few arise naturally from volcanoes and forest fires. They harm the environment through long-range transport and {{ref:nature-eco-689}}, which reconcentrates them to potentially dangerous levels.

Being halogenated and lipid soluble, they accumulate in fatty tissue, and concentrations rise up the {{ref:nature-eco-353}} as {{ref:nature-eco-690}}. Because wind and water carry them, POPs released in one country affect people and wildlife far away, including the Antarctic and the Arctic. For people not exposed through accident or work, over 90% of exposure comes from animal-product foods.

nature-econ-095.title: Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken
nature-econ-095.text:
A government that spends $840 billion on a war cannot also spend it on healthcare, education or tax cuts. That forgone alternative is the heart of opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others. It is the benefit you would have had from the second-best choice.

The idea expresses the link between {{ref:nature-found-051}} and choice, and its aim is efficient use of scarce resources. It counts all costs of a decision, explicit and implicit, and is not limited to money. Lost time, pleasure or any useful benefit also counts. Suppose someone leaves work for an hour to spend $200 on office supplies and earns $25 an hour. The $200 is the {{ref:nature-econ-096}} and the $25 of lost earnings the {{ref:nature-econ-124}}.

{{ref:nature-econ-148}}, already spent and unrecoverable, are excluded and should not sway present or future decisions. Every {{ref:nature-econ-099}} carries an opportunity cost, and a party that can produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others has a {{ref:nature-econ-106}} in it.

{{ref:nature-eco-140}} shows the same logic. {{ref:nature-eco-099}} protection carries opportunity costs such as old-growth timber that cannot be cut and {{ref:nature-eco-296}} that cannot be built on.

nature-econ-848.title: Capitalism: private property run for profit
nature-econ-848.text:
Capitalism is an {{ref:nature-econ-153}} built on private ownership of the means of production, run to obtain profit. Its constituent elements are {{ref:nature-econ-658}}, profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets, commodification, wage labor, and an emphasis on innovation and {{ref:nature-econ-478}}.

Capital accumulation is central: {{ref:nature-econ-604}}, as in {{ref:nature-econ-083}}, is invested for profit, then reinvested in further production in a continuous process. {{ref:nature-econ-478}} is a characteristic tendency of capitalist economies, which also swing through {{ref:nature-econ-870}} of expansion and recession.

There is no universally agreed definition, and it is unclear whether capitalism describes a whole society or only elements of one. Green variants exist. Eco-capitalism holds that natural capital, ecosystems with {{ref:nature-res-231}}, underlies all wealth, so governments should use market instruments such as a {{ref:nature-pol-081}} against environmental problems. Sustainable capitalism is a conceptual form built on sustainable practices that reduce externalities, though one account notes that a capitalist economy must expand to survive and find new markets.

nature-econ-849.title: Planned economy: allocation by economy-wide plan
nature-econ-849.text:
In a planned economy, investment, production and the allocation of capital goods, as in {{ref:nature-econ-083}}, follow economy-wide plans. Planning can be centralized, decentralized, participatory or Soviet-type. It contrasts with market economies, where autonomous firms decide production, pricing and investment. Market economies using indicative planning are called mixed economies or planned market economies.

Critics argue planners cannot detect consumer preferences, shortages and surpluses accurately enough. Mises and Hayek described this as the economic calculation problem and the local knowledge problem. Supporters argue the state can direct land, labor and capital to its objectives. In the 1930s Soviet Union, private consumption was forced down from 80% to 50% of {{ref:nature-econ-530}}.

nature-econ-864.title: Black markets: trade the law forbids
nature-econ-864.text:
{{ref:nature-res-139}} is, according to Interpol, an industry worth almost as much as drug production in some countries. It is one face of the black market: a clandestine market, or set of transactions, with some aspect of illegality within a legal jurisdiction. It is a {{ref:nature-econ-342}} that operates out of sight.

Transactions in goods whose production or distribution the law prohibits or restricts are black-market trade because the exchange itself is illegal. Such goods may be cheaper than legal ones because suppliers avoid production costs and taxes. In many developing countries wild animals are captured and sold as pets, or hunted for meat, hides and organs used in traditional medicine.

nature-econ-863.title: Barriers to entry: what keeps newcomers out
nature-econ-863.text:
A new firm often faces a cost that the firms already in the market never had to pay. That is a barrier to entry: a {{ref:nature-econ-307}} a new entrant must bear to enter a market that incumbents do not bear or have not had to bear.

By protecting incumbents and restricting competition, barriers can distort prices, which is why they matter most in antitrust policy. They often cause or help sustain a {{ref:nature-econ-349}} or oligopoly, or give firms market power. Governments can also erect them, for instance to meet consumer protection laws.

A primary barrier is a cost that is a barrier on its own. An ancillary barrier only reinforces other barriers that are present. A structural barrier comes from inherent industry conditions such as upfront capital, {{ref:nature-econ-303}} and {{ref:nature-pol-288}}. A strategic barrier is created or raised by existing firms, for example by exclusive contracts.

The height of barriers separates market types. {{ref:nature-econ-353}} has zero barriers to entry, {{ref:nature-econ-311}} allows medium barriers, and oligopoly typically has high ones. Porter classes markets by entry and exit barriers: the higher both are, the more prone a market is to {{ref:nature-econ-350}}, and the lower, the nearer to perfect competition.

Economists have offered conflicting definitions since the 1950s. Bain (1956), Stigler (1968), Fisher (1979), Baumol and Willig (1981) and others each gave one, and no consensus exists on which to use.

nature-econ-865.title: Public utilities: essential services under public control
nature-econ-865.text:
A public utility is an organization that maintains the infrastructure for a public service, often also providing the service itself. Utilities supply goods considered essential, such as water, gas, electricity, telephone and waste disposal, and are subject to public control or regulation.

The reason is the cost structure. Utilities are capital-intensive, with large {{ref:nature-econ-303}} and high {{ref:nature-econ-307}} for plants, lines and treatment facilities. Electricity transmission lines and natural gas pipelines have the traits of a {{ref:nature-econ-350}}: where infrastructure exists, competing brings little benefit. In the US, public utilities commissions regulate electric, gas, telecom, water and rail companies, approving or denying rate increases on behalf of ratepayers.

In 1996, FERC Order No. 888 required electric utilities to open their transmission systems and unbundle transmission from other operations. That restructured the regulated {{ref:nature-econ-349}} toward competition among bulk sellers.

Modern utilities may draw partly or wholly on clean and {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, mostly wind turbines and solar panels. In OECD countries, wholesale {{ref:nature-clim-282}} has become far more decentralised with solar and wind power, while distribution and transmission networks often stay centralised and need heavy government involvement.

nature-econ-859.title: Product differentiation: making one product stand apart
nature-econ-859.text:
Edward Chamberlin proposed the concept in his 1933 book on {{ref:nature-econ-311}}. Product differentiation is the process of distinguishing a product from competitors' and from a firm's other products to make it more attractive to a target market. It is inconsistent with perfect competition, which needs identical products.

Vertical differentiation rests on a characteristic consumers can rank objectively, such as quality. Horizontal differentiation rests on subjective taste, such as colour. Mixed differentiation combines both. Sources include quality, functional features or design, buyers' ignorance, advertising and availability in time and place. Buyers must perceive the difference. A green product may have lower environmental harm yet be inferior in other respects, so its appeal depends on advertising and social pressure.

The pricing effect is direct. A firm cannot charge a higher price if products are good substitutes, and the further a product departs from others in its segment, the higher the price it can charge. Low differentiation makes {{ref:nature-econ-857}} harder to hold, since a small price cut can win a large share of the market.

nature-econ-857.title: Collusion: when rivals quietly stop competing
nature-econ-857.text:
In 2019 the European Commission found that BMW, Daimler and Volkswagen had colluded to hold back improvements in vehicle emissions technology. Collusion is an agreement or secret cooperation among firms or individuals to limit competition, for example by dividing a market, fixing prices or limiting output.

It often arises in an {{ref:nature-econ-364}}. Price fixing harms consumers, so it is illegal under antitrust law and participants keep it secret. Tacit collusion is considered legal.

A collusive price is unsustainable in a one-off game because members have an incentive to deviate. It needs repeated interaction and firms that value future profits. With n symmetric firms, the cartel is stable only if the {{ref:nature-econ-747}} is at least (n-1)/n, so more firms make collusion harder to sustain. Other barriers include cost and demand differences and asymmetric information. High concentration, homogeneous products and stable demand or excess capacity favour it.

Governments respond with fines and imprisonment, screening markets for suspicious pricing, and leniency for the first firm to confess.

nature-econ-862.title: Vertical integration: owning the supply chain
nature-econ-862.text:
In the US, 90% of poultry, 69% of hogs and 29% of cattle are produced under contracts that act as vertical integration. It is an arrangement in which a company owns and controls several stages of its {{ref:nature-acct-118}}. It contrasts with horizontal integration, where a company produces several related items, and comes as backward (upstream), forward (downstream) or balanced.

A firm integrates to secure the supplies it needs and the market for its product. The real net output ratio, added value over total production value, measures it: the less a firm outsources, the closer the ratio is to one. Gains include synchronising supply and demand, capturing upstream or downstream margins and lower uncertainty. Losses include higher switching costs, weaker performance incentives upstream and specific investments.

For society, it can lower consumer prices by cutting intermediary markups, but it can enable price manipulation where market power is established, and it becomes undesirable when it turns anti-competitive.

Electricity shows both sides. Before late-20th-century {{ref:nature-val-108}}, most US electric utilities were vertically integrated across generation, transmission, distribution and sales. PURPA in 1978 forced them to buy outside power if competitive, giving rise to independent producers.

nature-econ-858.title: Bertrand competition: rivals undercutting down to cost
nature-econ-858.text:
If two firms sell the same good and compete on price, what happens? Bertrand proposed in 1883, as a reply to Cournot, that firms should undercut rivals' prices whenever those exceed marginal cost. Edgeworth formalised the idea in 1889. The model of oligopoly it produced has firms selling identical goods compete by setting prices, while buyers choose the quantities. It is the price-setting counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-302}}.

It assumes identical goods, equal marginal costs, no capacity limits, simultaneous price setting and no search costs, so the lowest-priced firm takes the whole market. The only equilibrium is price equal to marginal cost, with zero profit. It is a weak {{ref:nature-econ-718}} because deviating costs nothing.

Relax the assumptions and the result shifts. Product differentiation, transport or search costs remove the result that price falls to marginal cost. With capacity constraints (the Bertrand-Edgeworth model) a pure-strategy equilibrium may not exist, the Edgeworth paradox. With {{ref:nature-pol-288}}, firms may price aggressively to enlarge their customer base.

Bertrand industries are more competitive than Cournot ones because prices are strategic complements while quantities are strategic substitutes. Bertrand suits flexible capacity, and Cournot suits output set in advance.

nature-econ-861.title: Stackelberg competition: the advantage of moving first
nature-econ-861.text:
Heinrich von Stackelberg described this sequential game in 1934. A leader firm chooses its quantity first, and follower firms then respond, competing on quantity. It needs a leader with commitment power, and the follower must observe the leader's move and be unable to commit to other actions.

It is solved by {{ref:nature-econ-735}}: the leader anticipates the follower's best response and picks the quantity maximising its own payoff. Moving first gives the leader an advantage over {{ref:nature-econ-302}}. If the follower cannot observe the leader's move, the game reduces to that Cournot case.

Outcomes sit between the extremes. Stackelberg output exceeds Cournot output but is below Bertrand output, and its price is lower than Cournot's but higher than Bertrand's. Its price also lies below the monopoly or cartel price but above the perfectly competitive price.

nature-econ-850.title: Income distribution: who gets the national income
nature-econ-850.text:
Income distribution describes how a country's total income, or GDP, is shared among its population. Classical economists such as Smith, Malthus and Ricardo studied {{ref:nature-econ-493}} distribution, while modern economists focus on distribution across individuals and households. In neoclassical theory, national income is distributed according to factor prices, the payment to each factor of production.

Inequality is distinct from poverty and fairness. The {{ref:nature-econ-527}} measures it from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), and the {{ref:nature-econ-873}} can depict it. Policies that shape it include progressive taxation and public spending on education, healthcare and social security for lower-income groups.

The {{ref:nature-eecon-164}} holds that inequality rises as a country develops and falls once average income reaches a certain level, though many prominent economists disagree that rising inequality is necessary. Income mobility, how people move in the earnings hierarchy over their lifetime, is measured by the association between parents' and adult children's socioeconomic standing.

Institutions matter too. Unionization reduces wage inequality: for American male workers the reduction was 1.7 percent in the private sector and 16.2 percent in the public sector.
